title: A non-HTTP protocol's field becomes an identifier, and the monitoring daemon that watches that identifier re-parses it as a shell command
index_line: T-0024 · EXEC · SMTP-supplied name reaches a watch/alarm config that is shell-interpreted · perl/any monitoring · corroborated
invariant_violated: The mail path validates what it *delivers* and assumes the identifier it records is inert. But the identifier is handed to a monitoring daemon whose configuration language is a shell, so a name that is legal in one protocol is syntax in the other. The monitoring plane is treated as trusted because it is 'just alerting'.

mechanism.does: an unauthenticated request arrives over a non-HTTP protocol (SMTP envelope/recipient, or any field the primary service accepts before auth)
the service accepts the value and uses it as an *identifier* — a queue/mailbox/service name, logged and recorded
the identifier is handed to a monitoring/alerting component (watch daemon, trap notifier, status hook) that monitors items by name
the monitoring component builds its watch entry by string interpolation into a configuration line that is interpreted by a shell when the state changes
a state transition fires the watch, so the shell evaluates the whole line — including the identifier
the command runs as the service account, from a request that never authenticated

source.protocol.value: a non-HTTP protocol field — SMTP envelope/recipient, a queue name, a job label. The primary service's validation is written for that protocol, not for the shell

sink.exec.shell.value: the monitoring daemon's command execution (watch/alarm `execute`/`watchfor`, trap handler, status hook)

guard.escaping.value: protocol-level validation sits in front of the identifier and passes it; the shell layer has no escaping at all

encoding.shell.value: metacharacters that are legal in the identifier but syntactic to a shell — plus the trigger that must fire for the watch line to be evaluated

source.file.name.value: the alternative shape: the identifier is a filename/dirname the attacker chooses, which the monitor reports on

preconditions.expr: a monitoring/watch component consumes service identifiers and builds shell-interpreted config from them
the primary service is unauthenticated at the point the identifier is created (SMTP before auth, a public form, a queue producer)
the identifier reaches the monitor unchanged (no allow-list, no quoting) and a state transition will fire the watch
the monitor actually runs and its configuration is regenerated from service state (the optional package is installed and notification is enabled)

check.spec: ps -eo cmd | grep -E 'swatch|monit|zabbix' | grep -v grep; grep -ri 'snmp_notify' /opt/zimbra/conf 2>/dev/null

success: the daemon's own log carries the injected identifier inside the line it reports as a status change
a marker file or command output appears with the service account's uid
the effect requires a state transition, so the second request (the one that changes state) is the one that fires, not the first
failure_like: identifiers are quoted or allow-listed before reaching the monitor
the monitoring component is not installed / notifications disabled — the code path is absent, not merely unreachable
the watch line is evaluated by an exec that does not invoke a shell
false_positive: the payload echoed back in a log line proves the identifier was *stored*, not that it was *evaluated* — require the command's side effect
a metacharacter in a name that the mail layer rejects at SMTP time (5xx) never reaches the monitor

hazards: the primary protocol matters: validation written for HTTP or SMTP is almost never sufficient for a shell, and identifiers are the usual gap
two requests are needed (create the identifier, then change state to fire the watch) — a single-shot probe will look negative on a vulnerable host
the trigger may be a scheduled sweep rather than an event — plan for a wait, not a race
non_transfers: monitoring stacks that pass identifiers as argv (no shell) — argument injection may still apply (T-0005), but metacharacters do not
identifiers restricted to a fixed character class by the primary service before they are recorded
services where the monitor reads a machine interface (netlink, JSON API) rather than generating config text

evidence.target: Zimbra Collaboration Suite < 10.1.20 with zimbra-snmp + SNMP notifications (CVE-2026-73570)
